# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Obstetric emergencies, injuries, strokes and myocardial infarctions share a
geographical condition: the patient has to reach a hospital able to treat them
in time. The Lancet Commission on Global Surgery measured timely access as the
share of the population that can reach, within two hours, a facility able to
perform caesarean delivery, laparotomy and treatment of open fractures
[@meara2015], and the Lancet Global Health Commission on high-quality health
systems counted timely action among the components of competent care, with
access as a prerequisite for benefiting from it [@kruk2018]. Global friction surfaces have made it
possible to map travel time everywhere: about 8.9 % of the world population
cannot reach a health facility within one hour by motorized transport, and
43.3 % cannot on foot [@weiss2020]. National studies built on similar models
report, for instance, that 29.0 % of people in sub-Saharan Africa live more than
two hours from a public hospital [@ouma2018] and that access falls steeply from
cities to villages and dispersed rural areas [@florio2023].

These figures depend on how access is measured. Access is multidimensional
[@penchansky1981], and even its spatial component requires a chain of
decisions, a metric, an access model, a set of destinations and a population
unit with its weighting, each of which can change the result [@wang2012;
@neutens2015; @delamater2012]. In rural Haiti, five measures of access to public
hospitals correlated at 0.78 to 0.99, yet straight-line distance overstated the
population covered within a given threshold [@bhangdia2022].

Two gaps follow for national planning in low- and middle-income countries.
First, measures are usually compared through correlations, whereas the planning
output is a list: the districts classified as underserved. Two measures can rank
districts almost identically and still disagree on which ones cross a threshold.
Second, modeled travel time is rarely tested against an outcome it should
explain. Validation is typically internal, or against routing services that
share the same road data [@nelson2019]. In Spain, longer car travel time to
hospitals was associated with higher mortality, most clearly among older adults
and for time-sensitive causes [@perez2026]. Comparable tests in settings with
fragmented health systems and long travel times are scarce.

Peru is such a setting. Its territory spans a coastal desert, the Andes above
3,500 m and the lowland Amazon. Its health system runs separate networks for
the Ministry of Health and regional governments, the social-security insurer,
the armed forces and police, and private providers, and the extension of
coverage has long been its main challenge [@alcalde2011]. Two national
studies have modeled travel time to care. Carrasco-Escobar et al. [-@carrasco2020]
estimated village-level times to public facilities of three levels of care, but
did not weight by population or compare their estimates with other measures or
with observed journeys. Bocanegra-Becerra [-@bocanegra2025] estimated that
42.4 % of the population could not reach public neurosurgical care within four
hours. The 2025 census now provides population counts for every district.

This study addresses three questions. RQ1: how far, in person-weighted travel
time, do Peruvians live from the nearest public complex hospital, and where are
those beyond 60 and 120 minutes? RQ2: how much does the identification of
districts with deficient access depend on the metric, the population
aggregation, the access model and the destination set? RQ3: is the measure
associated with an independent outcome, death outside a health facility,
particularly for causes amenable to hospital care? The study contributes, first,
a reproducible district measure weighted by the 2025 census and checked against
an alternative routing engine; second, evidence that aggregation and the access
model, rather than the choice of destinations, change which districts are
flagged; and third, a pre-specified negative test that shows the limits of place
of death as a criterion for validating access measures. Deviations from the
version-controlled analysis plan are reported with their timing (Appendix A).

# Background {#sec-background}

## Why measures of access disagree

Distance-based measures summarize the impedance between a population and its
nearest facility; floating catchment measures add supply and competing demand.
The two-step floating catchment area method (2SFCA) computes a supply-to-demand
ratio within each facility's travel-time catchment and sums the ratios reachable
from each population location [@luo2003]. Proximity and availability need not
agree, and reviews ask that the choice be justified rather than assumed
[@wang2012; @neutens2015].

The population unit adds a second source of variation. Accessibility computed at
the centroid of an areal unit stands in for every resident of that unit. In
Montreal, centroid-based measures were accurate for most census tracts but erred
importantly for 5–10 % of them, mostly suburban tracts with unevenly spread
residents [@apparicio2008], and a later comparison found errors of the same order
[@apparicio2017]. Aggregation error arises whenever a single point stands for a
population spread across an area, and finer data on where people live reduce it
[@hewko2002]; it is the local form of the modifiable areal unit problem
[@openshaw1984]. Peru's districts range from city blocks to Amazonian
territories of thousands of square kilometers, so the problem cannot be assumed
away.

## Validating national travel-time maps

Friction surfaces convert land cover, roads, slope and water into the time
needed to cross each cell and accumulate cost from the destinations
[@weiss2020]. Against Google driving directions, global accessibility estimates
were shorter in most journeys, with a median difference of $-16.9$ %
[@nelson2019]. Women in rural Rwanda reported journeys to a district hospital
1.49 times longer than modeled [@rudolfson2020], and in Lagos replicated drives
to emergency obstetric care took a median of 50 minutes, against 5 minutes from
a friction surface and 11 from OpenStreetMap routing [@bankethomas2021].
Agreement in ranking does not imply agreement in minutes, and the error is
largest in congested cities and where transport is not motorized.

## Access and where people die

Most death registration systems record the place of death, and studies of
end-of-life care use it as an indicator. Its determinants reach well beyond
distance: among people with cancer, home death is associated with low functional
status, patient preference, home care and family support [@gomes2006], and in
Latin America with older age, lower education and, in some countries, rural
residence [@cordoba2026]. In Peru, 41.3 % of deaths registered between 2017 and
2024 occurred at home, with marked differences by insurance, education,
ethnicity and department [@mirandachavez2026]. Whether modeled travel time adds
to these determinants has not been tested in Peru; if it does, place of death
could serve as an external check on access measures, the test RQ3 sets out.

# Study area and data {#sec-data}

Peru had 32,706,028 counted residents in 1,893 districts in the 2025 census
[@inei2026]. <!-- claim-16 --> Districts are the smallest political-administrative
unit, and they are highly unequal in size and population. The
analysis combines eight data sources (Table @tbl-data). Destinations are public
complex hospitals, defined as Ministry of Health and regional-government
facilities of category II-1 or above in the national registry of health
establishments [@renipress2026]; the registry lists their institution, category
and coordinates. Population counts come from the census and are distributed
within districts with the 2025 WorldPop constrained grid [@bondarenko2025]. Travel time uses the 2020 motorized and walking-only friction
surfaces of the Malaria Atlas Project [@weiss2020]. District polygons come from
the Common Operational Dataset of administrative boundaries [@ocha2025]: of the
1,893 census districts, 21 have no polygon (294,298 residents, mostly districts
created after 2017) and one polygon, a boundary area between Mazamari and
Pangoa, has no census row. District mean altitude comes from the Copernicus
DEM [@esa2022]. The analysis therefore covers 1,872 districts and
32,411,730 people, 99.1 % of the counted population. <!-- claim-16 --> Deaths
come from the national online death certificate system [@sinadef2026], whose
national roll-out is described by Vargas-Herrera et al. [-@vargas2018].

# Methods {#sec-methods}

Fig. @fig-workflow summarizes the workflow; every number, figure and table comes
from the outputs of a version-controlled pipeline.

![Data sources, measurement, checks and the three research questions.](media/Fig1_workflow.pdf){#fig-workflow width=1}

## Destinations and population

Destinations are the hospitals of the Ministry of Health and regional
governments, the public network open to the general population; the other
networks serve affiliates or charge fees and enter only as sensitivity
variants. Of the 182 geolocated
public complex hospitals, 172 lay inside their district polygon and 7 within
20 km of its boundary; two lay more than 200 km away because of coordinate
errors and were excluded, and re-placing them at their district centroid changed
the 60-minute class of 1.12 % of districts (pre-specified limit 5 %). One
belonged to a district without a polygon. <!-- claim-17, claim-3 --> The 180
hospitals of the main set occupy 174 grid cells. <!-- claim-17 --> Census counts
were allocated to the cells of a 30 arc-second grid (about 927 m) in proportion
to the WorldPop estimates, so that each district keeps its census total exactly.

## Travel time and district summaries

We computed travel time from every cell to the nearest hospital as a
multi-source accumulated cost over the motorized friction surface with
Dijkstra's algorithm [@dijkstra1959; @virtanen2020], correcting cell widths for
latitude and resampling the friction by nearest neighbor. For each district we
report the person-weighted mean travel time, the share of residents in cells
beyond 60 and 120 minutes, the district-weighted mean, and the share of people
in districts whose person-weighted mean exceeds each threshold, the unit at
which planning lists are drawn. Sixty minutes is the main threshold, as in
global reporting [@weiss2020]; 120 minutes, the surgical benchmark
[@meara2015], is secondary because the routing check agreed weakly on that
class. Districts are grouped by the Amazon basin [HydroBASINS level 4,
@lehner2013] and by mean altitude: below 500 m, 500–2,500 m, and the high
(2,500–3,500 m) and very high ($\geq$ 3,500 m) classes of Barry and Pollard
[-@barry2003].

## Convergent check against routing

We routed a pre-specified sample of 200 district centroids, stratified by
quintile of travel time, by car to their three nearest hospitals with OSRM
[@luxen2011] and kept the shortest time; an enriched sample of 150 districts
with mean travel time above 45 minutes probes the remote tail. Both engines rest
on OpenStreetMap roads [@osm2026], so the check is of convergent, not
independent, validity. The pre-specified rule required a Spearman correlation of
at least 0.80 outside the Amazon, then proxied by five departments; the basin
split is post hoc. Six pairs of departmental capitals were compared in the same
way.

## Sensitivity to the measure (RQ2)

We compared ten variants with the main measure: straight-line distance from the
district centroid and population-weighted; travel time at the district's center
cell, which isolates aggregation (the pre-specified test of whether population
weighting matters, refuted if Spearman $\geq$ 0.95); travel time multiplied by
the OSRM-to-friction ratio of its trip-length band; three wider destination sets
(adding social-security hospitals, all complex hospitals and uncategorized
hospital-like facilities); walking time; and a 2SFCA score [@luo2003] with 60-
and 120-minute catchments, supply equal to the number of hospitals in each cell
of a grid four times coarser, read as a person-weighted district mean. For each
we report Spearman's correlation with a bootstrap 95 % CI over districts,
Kendall's tau, the Jaccard overlap of the 100 worst-access districts, and
Cohen's kappa [@cohen1960] for the deficient-access class at 60 and
120 minutes. Variants in minutes use the same thresholds; the others flag the
same number of districts as the main measure, so that kappa compares
classifications rather than units. Under the pre-specified criterion, Spearman
$\geq$ 0.95 together with kappa $\geq$ 0.90 for straight-line distance would
have shown that travel time adds nothing to it.

## Need and spatial structure

Need is the sum of the z-scores of the census shares of residents aged 60 or
over and aged 5 or over with a disability. A district is high-need if the sum is
positive and has deficient access if its person-weighted mean exceeds
60 minutes; a composite ranking was to be reported only if Kendall's tau across
five weighting schemes reached 0.80. Clustering of travel time was tested with
global Moran's I and local indicators of spatial association [@anselin1995]
under queen contiguity and four and eight nearest neighbors, with 9,999
permutations and false-discovery-rate control [@benjamini1995], in PySAL
[@rey2022].

## External outcome test (RQ3)

The outcome is death outside a health facility (at home, on a public road or in
another non-facility place) among deaths registered in 2022–2025, assigned to
the district of residence. The main population, fixed before the death records
were read, is deaths from causes amenable to timely hospital care, adapted from
the concept of amenable mortality [@nolte2003]: acute (myocardial infarction,
stroke, obstetric causes) and chronic (diabetes, hypertensive disease, chronic
lower respiratory disease, chronic kidney disease). H3a states that longer
travel time raises the odds of dying outside a facility; H3b, that the gradient
is steeper for acute causes. We fitted a logistic regression with department
fixed effects and district-clustered standard errors, giving a
population-averaged odds ratio per 60 minutes adjusted for age group, sex (as
recorded on the death certificate: male, female or not recorded), cause group
and district mean altitude [@cameron2015; @mundlak1978]. Sensitivity
analyses comprise an exchangeable generalized estimating equation
[@liang1986], the exclusion of low-completeness districts or of the
unclassified "other place" category, the period 2020–2021, a within-department
permutation placebo and cancer deaths as a negative control. A known-truth
simulation with district random intercepts estimated the false-positive rate,
bias and coverage of the estimator [@morris2019]; the plan required a
false-positive rate of at most 7 % for confirmatory use.

## Analysis plan, deviations and software

The plan was frozen in a version-controlled file before any access result was
computed and amended in dated versions. It was not deposited in a public
registry, so we call it pre-specified rather than pre-registered; Appendix A
lists each deviation with its timing. Two machine-learning checks were
subordinate: a ridge calibration of the OSRM-to-friction ratio, used only as a
sensitivity variant, and a gradient-boosting test of whether travel time
improves the prediction of place of death, both validated by leaving one
department out [@roberts2017; @ploton2020]. Models used statsmodels
[@seabold2010] and scikit-learn [@pedregosa2011]. Code, cached routing responses
and the notebook that reproduces every output are archived in a public
repository (reference withheld for anonymized review).

DeepSeek (DeepSeek-AI) was consulted to debug errors and to refactor redundant
code blocks in the pipeline; every change it suggested was reviewed, executed
and verified by the authors against the frozen plan, the cached routing
responses and the project test suite, and the authors take full responsibility
for the final code and the results it produces.

# Results {#sec-results}

## How far people live from a public complex hospital {#sec-res-rq1}

The person-weighted mean travel time to the nearest public complex hospital was
37.8 minutes; 10.9 % of residents lived in cells more than 60 minutes away and
4.6 % more than 120 minutes away. Weighting every district equally raised the
mean to 91.6 minutes, because the most remote districts are small. The share
also depends on the unit that is classified: 12.5 % of people lived in districts
whose person-weighted mean exceeded 60 minutes, and 5.5 % in districts above
120 minutes. <!-- claim-1, claim-3 --> On foot, 46.5 % of residents lived more
than 60 minutes from such a hospital, and the person-weighted mean was
226.8 minutes. <!-- claim-14 -->

Long travel times concentrate where few people live (Fig. @fig-access a). Within
60 minutes, coverage was 93.1 % below 500 m, 88.2 % at 2,500–3,500 m, 85.6 % at
3,500 m or more and 83.8 % at 500–2,500 m; the last band, which spans inter-Andean
valleys and the forested slopes towards the Amazon, also had the lowest
coverage within 120 minutes (91.9 %, Fig. @fig-access b). <!-- claim-22 --> The
very high Andes differ in a subtler way: only 66.0 % of their residents were
within 30 minutes, the lowest of any band, but 97.4 % were within two hours.
<!-- claim-22 --> Inside the Amazon basin, 22.8 % of residents lived more than
60 minutes away, against 5.6 % outside it, and in the lowland basin below 500 m
the person-weighted mean reached 274.2 minutes (Table @tbl-equity).
<!-- claim-23 -->

## Agreement with routing {#sec-res-osrm}

Of the 200 pre-specified centroids, 199 were routed, and friction and OSRM times
correlated at Spearman 0.738. Outside the five Amazon departments, where the
pre-specified rule applied, the correlation was 0.801 (95 % CI 0.733–0.854,
n = 174): the point estimate met the threshold, but the interval crosses it.
Split by the HydroBASINS basin, agreement was 0.850 outside (n = 86) and 0.653
inside (n = 113), and it fell to 0.400 in the enriched remote sample (n = 149;
Supplementary Table S1). <!-- claim-2 --> OSRM times exceeded friction times in
the pre-specified sample (median ratio 1.17) but fell short of them in the
lowland basin (0.82), where the friction surface lacks river transport and OSRM
snaps centroids to the nearest road. <!-- claim-18 --> Agreement on the
120-minute class was weak (kappa 0.342). <!-- claim-1 --> Between six pairs of
departmental capitals the engines differed by 18.0 % on average
(Supplementary Fig. S1). <!-- claim-18 -->

## Which districts each measure flags {#sec-res-rq2}

The destination set barely mattered (Spearman 0.991–0.993 and kappa at
60 minutes 0.978–0.990; Table @tbl-rq2); the other choices mattered more.
<!-- claim-10 -->

Straight-line distance ranked districts much as travel time did (Spearman 0.902
from the centroid and 0.923 population-weighted) but agreed less on who is
deficient. When each flagged the same 746 districts at 60 minutes, kappa was
0.739 and 0.777, and the top-100 worst-access sets overlapped by only 0.429 and
0.351. <!-- claim-9 --> In the population-weighted comparison, 100 districts were
flagged by travel time alone and another 100 by straight-line distance alone,
the latter cut at the matched distance of 33.1 km (Fig. @fig-methods).
<!-- claim-19 --> The two groups lie in different terrain: 79 of the districts
flagged only by travel time are in the Amazon basin and 52 lie at 500–2,500 m,
whereas 57 of those flagged only by distance lie at 3,500 m or more.
<!-- claim-19 -->

Aggregation changed the count more than the ranking: travel time at the
district's center cell correlated with the person-weighted measure at 0.810,
below the 0.95 at which the simpler measure would have sufficed, yet flagged
1,010 districts instead of 746 at 60 minutes and 537 instead of 235 at
120 minutes. <!-- claim-13 --> Walking time ranked districts like motorized time
(0.958) but flagged 1,686 of the 1,872 districts at the same threshold.
<!-- claim-14 -->

The catchment model departed furthest (Spearman 0.524 and 0.306 with 60- and
120-minute catchments; kappa 0.539 and 0.271). With the 60-minute catchment,
14.9 % of districts, holding 4.2 % of the population, had no hospital within
reach. <!-- claim-11 --> Under the pre-specified criteria, straight-line distance
did not reproduce the travel-time classification, and population weighting was
not redundant.

## Need and spatial structure {#sec-res-need}

Combining need with access, 371 districts, home to 739,935 people (2.3 % of the
population), were high-need with deficient access (Fig. @fig-need); 86.3 % of
them lie at 2,500 m or more. <!-- claim-12, claim-21 --> Membership of this group
was stable across the five need-weighting schemes (97.3 %), but the need index
itself was not: the minimum Kendall's tau against the equal-weight ranking was
0.729, below the 0.80 the plan required, so we report membership and no
composite ranking. Travel time was strongly clustered (global Moran's I 0.662
with queen contiguity, 0.656 and 0.547 with four and eight neighbors; p = 0.0001
with 9,999 permutations), but the number of significant local clusters varied
from 235 to 456 districts across neighborhood definitions, so local clusters
are not reported as findings. <!-- claim-12 -->

![Need and access by district. Need: sum of z-scores of the shares aged 60 or over and with a disability; deficient access: mean travel time above 60 min. The key gives districts and share of the population per class; the blank polygon has no census row. Map lines delineate study areas and do not necessarily depict accepted national boundaries.](media/Fig4_need_access.pdf){#fig-need width=0.46}

## Travel time and dying outside a facility {#sec-res-rq3}

Of 601,092 deaths registered in 2022–2025, 593,438 entered the model frame and
590,654 had the district resolved by name; 70,496 of these were due to amenable
causes. <!-- claim-20 --> Among amenable deaths, travel time was not associated
with dying outside a facility (odds ratio per 60 minutes 1.005, 95 % CI
0.986–1.025, p = 0.607; placebo p = 0.61; Fig. @fig-rq3). <!-- claim-4, claim-20 -->
The estimate stayed near one without low-completeness districts or the "other
place" category and in 2020–2021. The exchangeable GEE gave 0.992 (0.977–1.009),
of opposite sign, so the pre-specified "same sign" criterion was not met,
although neither estimator detected an association. Acute and chronic gradients
did not differ (1.000 and 1.020; interaction p = 0.251; Supplementary Table S4).
<!-- claim-24 -->

![Odds ratios of dying outside a health facility per 60 minutes of travel time (95 % CIs): H3a and its sensitivity analyses, H3b, other cause groups and all causes (exploratory). Dashed line: odds ratio planted in the simulation.](media/Fig5_rq3.pdf){#fig-rq3 width=1}

Over all causes the odds ratio was 1.037 (1.023–1.052), but this exploratory
gradient came from the residual "other" group (1.053, 1.034–1.071), and cancer,
the negative control, gave a similar estimate (1.032, 0.978–1.090).
<!-- claim-5 --> The simulation bounds the interpretation: the estimator's
false-positive rate was 7.6 % (Monte Carlo SE 1.2 %), above the pre-specified
7 %, and it covered a planted odds ratio of 1.10 in 90.0 % of replications,
detecting it with power 0.99 (Supplementary Table S2); by the plan's rule the
model is used descriptively. <!-- claim-6, claim-24 --> The cause was unknown
more often for deaths outside facilities, most of all near hospitals (22.5 %
against 12.9 % in facilities within 30 minutes; 11.3 % against 9.1 % beyond
120 minutes; Supplementary Table S5). <!-- claim-15 --> If those deaths are
amenable in similar proportion across travel times, excluding them steepens
rather than flattens the gradient. Travel time also added no predictive value
among amenable deaths in a gradient-boosting model (Supplementary Table S3).
<!-- claim-8 -->

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

## Aggregation and the access model change the list of underserved districts

The headline is robust to the definition of destinations and fragile to the
choices that define the population and the access model. This ordering matches
studies of urban health services, where straight-line and network distances
correlated above 0.90 but the choice of accessibility measure changed the
assessment most [@apparicio2008; @apparicio2017], and Delamater et al.
[-@delamater2012], whose raster and network models located the same
limited-access areas but counted different numbers of people in them. Peru
magnifies the aggregation component. Centroid-based measures erred for 5–10 % of
census tracts in Montreal; here, reading time at district centers flagged 264
more districts at 60 minutes than weighting by where people live, because large
Andean and Amazonian districts concentrate their population in a valley or along
a river while their geometric center lies in empty terrain. <!-- claim-13 -->
Correlations alone would have hidden this, as Bhangdia et al. [-@bhangdia2022]
warned for highly correlated measures that disagree on coverage. The
disagreement is also geographically structured: travel time adds districts on
the forested Andean slopes, where distance understates the cost of crossing
terrain, and straight-line distance adds districts on the high plateau, where
roads make travel faster than distance suggests. <!-- claim-19 -->

The catchment model answers a different question. 2SFCA rewards districts whose
catchment holds several hospitals relative to its population, so a district one
hour from a single hospital that serves a large city can score lower than a
remote district near a small one. Florio et al. [-@florio2023] found geographic
access in sub-Saharan Africa constrained mainly by travel impedance rather than
facility density; in Peru, proximity and availability rank districts differently
(Spearman 0.306–0.524), so a priority list should state which of the two it
targets. <!-- claim-11 -->

## What the routing check can and cannot show

The friction surface ranked districts consistently with OSRM outside the Amazon,
at the pre-specified threshold, but agreement weakened in the remote tail and the
lowland basin, where the surface lacks river transport and OSRM ignores the leg
from a centroid to the nearest road. Because both engines rely on OpenStreetMap,
their agreement is convergent evidence, not independent validation, and external
studies suggest that both underestimate real journeys: self-reported times were
1.49 times the modeled ones in rural Rwanda [@rudolfson2020], and modeled times
in Lagos fell far short of replicated drives [@bankethomas2021]. Our minutes
should therefore be read as optimistic for people without a vehicle and for
river-dependent districts, and the 120-minute class as indicative only;
walking times give the other bound. <!-- claim-1 -->

## Why place of death did not validate access

The external test did not find the gradient specific to amenable causes that a
valid access measure should produce, and three explanations fit the data. Place of death may be a poor marker of
geographic access in Peru, shaped as it is by insurance, education, ethnicity,
preference and palliative-care needs [@mirandachavez2026; @gomes2006]; in Latin
America home death is linked more consistently to age and education than to
rurality [@cordoba2026]. Exposure is measured at the district of residence rather
than on each patient's journey, an assignment subject to the uncertain geographic
context problem [@kwan2012] that dilutes individual associations, and the
simulation did not model that dilution. And the measure may err most where an
association would be strongest, in the remote tail. Pérez et al. [-@perez2026]
found hospital travel time associated with mortality in Spain, with universal
coverage and a mortality outcome rather than the place of death of those who
died; together, the two results suggest that place of death is a weak criterion
for validating access measures. The null is informative within its precision:
the interval excludes an odds ratio of 1.10 per hour, which the simulation
detected with power 0.99, but not smaller associations, and the estimator's
false-positive rate exceeded the pre-specified limit. <!-- claim-4, claim-6 -->

## Implications for planning

Three rules follow for agencies that rank districts for hospital investment.
Population-weighted travel time should replace straight-line distance and
centroid-based measures when lists are drawn, because those produce different
lists, not slightly different rankings. Lists should state the access model they
assume, since proximity and availability point to different districts. And the
371 high-need districts with deficient access, mostly above 2,500 m, are a
defensible starting set because their membership was stable across need
weightings, although no composite ranking within it is warranted.
<!-- claim-12, claim-21 --> These rules rest on RQ1 and RQ2; RQ3 gives no basis
for prioritizing districts by place of death.

## Limitations

The friction surface dates from 2020, whereas hospitals are listed as of 2026
and deaths span 2022–2025, so openings and closures in between are not
represented. Hospitals without coordinates in the registry could not be placed,
and the 21 census districts without a polygon (294,298 residents) are excluded;
dropping the 12 provinces that contain them changed the share beyond 60 minutes
from 10.9 % to 10.6 %. <!-- claim-3, claim-16 --> The 2SFCA counts hospitals,
not beds or specialists, on a coarser grid, and category II-1 or above reflects
registry category rather than the services actually available. The routing check
used a public demo server whose data date is not published, although its
responses are archived. Registration completeness varies across districts, but
its correlation with travel time was weak, and the place of death is missing or
unclassified for a minority of records. All results are ecological and refer to
districts, not to individuals.

# Conclusions {#sec-conclusions}

This study measured, for every Peruvian district, how long residents take to
reach a public complex hospital, weighting a national friction surface by where
the 2025 census places them. About one resident in ten lives more than an hour
away, and the burden falls on the Amazon basin and the forested slopes between
the Andes and the lowland. <!-- claim-1, claim-22 --> Methodologically, who counts
as far from hospital care depends less on which hospitals are counted than on
how the population is aggregated and how access is modeled: weighting by where
people live rather than by district centers changes the list of deficient
districts by about a third, and a floating catchment measure orders districts
differently. <!-- claim-13, claim-11 --> These choices decide which places enter
a planning list and should be stated whenever one is published. Substantively,
travel time was not associated with dying outside a facility among deaths
amenable to hospital care; place of death proved a weak yardstick for access,
and validating access measures in Peru will require outcomes closer to
time-critical care, such as obstetric emergencies or trauma, and exposures
measured on the journeys patients actually make.
